title: AI Conversations Are Texts. Teach Them That Way.
author: Mike Kentz
summary: Kentz reframes AI conversations as a new genre of text that deserves explicit literacy instruction. Students increasingly use generative AI to explore ideas, brainstorm, and develop thinking—yet they often lack the scaffolding to do this effectively. The problem is not whether AI should be used (it will be) but how to teach students to use it as a thinking tool rather than a shortcut. AI conversations are texts with conventions: clarity of prompt matters, iterative refinement produces better outputs, context shapes results, and the best use is exploratory rather than solution-seeking. By teaching students to analyze, revise, and learn from AI interactions the way they would learn from writing, teachers equip them to leverage AI in service of genuine learning. Kentz advocates treating AI conversations as compositions: students write prompts, receive outputs, refine prompts based on results, and analyze what worked and why. This mirrors classical writing instruction where drafting, feedback, and revision build skill. The method makes visible the thinking process that AI can support but not replace. Students learn that garbage in produces garbage out, that specificity matters, and that the conversation itself is the learning artifact—not the final output. This approach integrates AI use into sound pedagogical practice rather than treating it as a disruptive force to be banned or contained.
points: AI conversations are a new genre of text with their own conventions: clarity, iterative refinement, context awareness, and exploratory mindset are essential.
Teaching students to use AI as a thinking tool requires the same writing pedagogy (drafting, feedback, revision) applied to prompts and interactions, not the final output.
The learning artifact is the conversation and the thinking process, not the AI-generated text—this shift prevents students from offloading thinking to the system.
Specificity in prompts matters: vague prompts produce vague results, teaching students the consequence of unclear communication.
By integrating AI literacy into writing instruction, teachers acknowledge reality and leverage AI to deepen thinking rather than bypass it.
